chapter: The union and the 1920s-30s band scene
title: Who led Local 767: Press Johnson, Robinson and Marshall Royal's father
summary: Collette and Howard try to recall the union's early presidents; Press Johnson, a businessman named Robinson and Marshall Royal's father (secretary) come up.

story.theme_name: The musicians' union: cards, locals, and the Black-white merger
story.community_name: The musicians' union: cards, scale and the black-white merger

blocks.x: Yeah. Do you remember who was president in those times? Do any of those names come to you?
I knew people like Leo Davis and Press Johnson, but I didn't know much other than those.
Well, did you know Papa Mutt?
I knew who Papa Mutt was. Was he president for awhile, too?
I know who Papa Mutt was.
But Press Johnson (inaudible) Carl Johnson, or that was his son?
What was the father's name? It was Johnson, but I --
Press Johnson. That's what they called him, just Press.
And, naturally, Leo Davis I knew, he was a saxophone player.

And did you know -- there's one other person I want to know did you know real well. But he's not -- his name doesn't come to me right now, but it will in a few minutes. Now, if we'll shut this machine off for a minute, --

No, I don't know him, but his name is in the book, here. Now, we were trying to find out who started the union, 767, the musicians union in Los Angeles, the black union. Now, you mentioned -- what was his name?
Well, we've mentioned Robinson, but Robinson didn't start it.
No, I can't remember anybody else.
Wasn't he president at the time?
(Inaudible.) He was a businessman. He had some kind of a business there on --
You know, you used to go in the back and pay your dues.
I can't remember what he -- the only thing I know about him, he was just getting in there.
I didn't know that -- this was in twenty -- (Inaudible.)
Because he had Marshall Royal, and his --
His father or the uncle, because they were all musicians.
Maybe there we've got a key.
Wasn't Mr. Royal one of the -- wasn't he president at the time?
Uh-uh. But he was secretary. That's what he was, secretary.
The uncle was also a musician, though, wasn't he? I didn't know what his name was.

He had an uncle in the -- yeah. He was crippled, and that's one reason why he didn't do nothing, because he was crippled. He was something. Them things get away from me. I had to say that. I'm sorry to say that, but that's the way --
Oh, you've been doing very good. That's fine.
Well, we will sort of hit some other
periods and we'll come back to that. And if you think of anything, we'll get it down.
